description: The cable snaps and the elevator falls: can you save yourself by jumping at the very last second? We test three cases: a 15-floor fall (165 ft) standing still, the same fall with a perfectly timed jump, then a 3-floor fall (33 ft) with the same jump.
Standing still, the rider hits the bottom at 70 mph. With the best possible jump, he still hits at 63 mph. From 3 floors, the jump takes him from 31 mph to 24 mph: still a hard crash.

Why: you fall with the elevator, at the same speed. A jump only pushes you up at the speed of a jump, about 7 mph for the best human jump. Free fall from 165 ft gives v = √(2gh) = 70 mph, so the jump leaves 63 mph. It also has to be timed to a fraction of a second, with no way to see the bottom coming. MythBusters tested the myth in 2004 ('Elevator of Death') and busted it.
In real life this is very unlikely: elevators hang on several cables and have automatic safety brakes that stop a falling car.
This video is a 3D simulation (Blender): the fall follows v = √(2gh), the jump speed is 7 mph (C. S. Baird, West Texas A&M University, 2012).
sources_detail: MythBusters season 2, episode 17 'Elevator of Death' (6 Oct 2004): the myth that jumping at the last moment saves you in a falling elevator is busted (mythresults.com/episode17).

C. S. Baird, 'If I'm on an elevator that breaks loose and plummets down the shaft, can I avoid harm by jumping at the last second?', Science Questions with Surprising Answers, West Texas A&M University, 5 Dec 2012: maximum human jump velocity 7 mph; 165 ft (about 15 floors) and 33 ft (about 3 floors); 'jumping at the last moment would help, but not much'. Baird rounds to 72 to 65 mph and 31 to 25 mph.

On screen, computed with free fall v = √(2gh), g = 9.81 m/s², 1 floor = 11 ft: 165 ft = 50.29 m gives 31.41 m/s = 70.3 mph (shown 70); minus 7 mph = 63.3 mph (63). 33 ft = 10.06 m gives 14.05 m/s = 31.4 mph (31); minus 7 = 24.4 mph (24). Air drag neglected (small below about 200 km/h, The Conversation, 'I've always wondered').
